stories.headline: Messi vs. Ronaldo, Man Utd hire Moyes: GTA V came out in a different soccer world
stories.summary: As Grand Theft Auto VI is finally unleashed, here is what was happening in the world of soccer when the previous game was released 13 years ago
stories.body:
Given that it's the only thing anybody appears to be talking about, you may be aware that a new video game by the name of "Grand Theft Auto VI" was released on Thursday, thus ending a long and arduous 13-year wait among fans of the infamous Rockstar Games franchise for a new instalment.

The previous game in the series, GTA V, was launched what feels like an eon ago during the primordial mists of September 2013. Almost a decade-and-a-half later, GTA VI is finally upon us.

We couldn't help but ponder just how the soccer landscape has changed during those intervening years -- or not, as the case may be.

- Mr. Worldwide: Meet soccer star who's played for clubs on 6 continents

- MrBeast, meet Haaland: Man City star puts YouTuber through gauntlet

- Why Champions League's iconic 'star' match ball may soon be replaced

Spain were top of the world
One thing which is the same as it was in 2013 is Spain's dominance over men's international competition. On the release of GTA V, La Roja were reigning world and European champions after winning the UEFA European Championship in 2008 and 2012, either side of their triumph at the 2010 FIFA World Cup, in an unprecedented era of back-to-back-to-back glory.

Skip forward 13 years and Spain -- inspired by the likes of Lamine Yamal -- are back on top having emerged triumphant at both Euro 2024 and the 2026 World Cup. And now Spain's women's team is along for the ride, too, winning the Women's World Cup in 2023 and heading into next year's tournament as favorites.

Peak Lionel Messi vs. Cristiano Ronaldo
Excelling on either side of the Clásico divide, Lionel Messi and Cristiano Ronaldo were at the peak of their respective powers in 2013 at Barcelona and Real Madrid respectively. Messi had already won four Ballon d'Ors to Ronaldo's two (those tallies are now eight and five), and no fewer than 19 trophies with Barça compared to the three Ronaldo had won with Madrid at that point.

However, both heavyweights were putting up utterly ridiculous numbers: Messi had scored a remarkable 91 goals in the previous calendar year, while Ronaldo would end the season with a record 17 goals in a single UEFA Champions League campaign as Madrid ended their long wait for a 10th European crown.

They may have both now retired from international football, but Messi and Ronaldo are still active 13 years on. Messi is looking to lead Inter Miami CF to a second MLS title, while Ronaldo is nearing the end of his quest for 1,000 career goals at Saudi Pro League club Al Nassr.

Man United's post-Sir Alex Ferguson era had just begun
As hard as it may be to believe, Manchester United were the reigning Premier League champions when GTA V was released, with legendary manager Sir Alex Ferguson having just bowed out after spending over quarter of a century at the helm at Old Trafford.

David Moyes had been hand-picked as Ferguson's successor and, quite honestly, things have been going steadily downhill since then. United have just appointed their seventh permanent manager since Fergie's departure by poaching former United States men's national team boss Mauricio Pochettino, who was in his second-ever managerial role at Southampton when GTA V was launched.

Pep Guardiola at Bayern Munich, José Mourinho back at Chelsea
When it comes to the other modern giants of the managerial realm, Guardiola was just a few games into his new job as head coach at Bayern Munich in September 2013 having brought his successful stint at Barcelona to a close the previous year.

Pep's erstwhile nemesis, Mourinho, had returned to Chelsea after leaving Real Madrid under a big, sulky cloud. The Portuguese would go on to add another Premier League and League Cup double (in 2014-15) to his trophy tally at Stamford Bridge before subsequently leaving the club in December 2015 under a big, sulky cloud. Now he's back at Madrid, who knows how it will end?

Man City only had one Premier League title
After winning their first Premier League title in 2011-12, Manchester City were just about to embark on a period of dominance over the English top flight when GTA V was released. Beginning with the 2013-14 championship, the club gobbled up seven further titles (six of which were won under Guardiola) and a coveted Champions League trophy over the next decade.

Guardiola has since vacated his post at the Etihad, and the validity of City's sustained success is in the balance as they await punishment for being found guilty of over 100 serious breaches of the Premier League's financial regulations.

Mikel Arteta was still playing
He may be a Premier League-winning manager these days, but Mikel Arteta was still playing for Arsenal back in September 2013, rather than guiding them to titles. The Spaniard was at the tail end of his career but was still making regular appearances at the heart of the Gunners' midfield.

While the club would have to wait for Arteta to transition into management before ending their 22-year wait for a Premier League title, he did at least help tide them over with two consecutive FA Cups (2013-14 and 2014-15) before hanging up his boots.

Harry Kane had just got off the mark
It took him a while to get going, but striker Harry Kane had already opened his account for Tottenham Hotspur by the time GTA V was released. He scored his first-ever senior goal for the club during a UEFA Europa League game in the 2011-12 season.

Various loans and injuries meant that the young striker didn't score his first Premier League goal for the club until 2014, but he quickly set about making up for lost time, becoming both Spurs' and England's all-time top goal-scorer in the intervening years.

Now scoring for fun at Bayern, Kane is quickly ascending the German club's all-time scorers list and, by virtue of rattling through 61 goals in 51 games last season, also won the Ballon d'Or last month.

Portland Thorns had just won inaugural NWSL title
Having been established the previous year, 2013 saw the inaugural season of the National Women's Soccer League -- i.e, the top division of women's soccer in the U.S.

After finishing third in the regular season, the Portland Thorns came good in the championship playoffs. They beat the now-defunct Western New York Flash to win the first ever NWSL championship title, with a young Alex Morgan finishing the campaign as their leading goal-scorer.

The Thorns have also added two further titles to their honor roll since then, in 2017 and 2022 respectively.

stories.headline: Which of these 15 pass catchers should you trust going forward?
stories.summary: A look at wide receivers and tight ends who have become start-worthy, and others you should expect less from.
stories.body:
With the fantasy football trade deadline looming (Dec. 2), I'll have a column next week on the top candidates to move. So, to build up to the deadline, this is a good opportunity to write about my current trust levels with pass catchers in the league.

These are wide receivers and tight ends that are trending up and those who are starting to lose my trust based on their usage, route deployment and declining production. I'm not saying there are cut candidates in here, as most players still have some level of value, but the point of the column is to give managers the data and analysis they need to make lineup decisions in the critical weeks ahead.

There are 15 players below broken down into four separate categories: pass catchers to trust, not to trust, those to expect less from and also a couple deeper-league targets.

Pass catchers to trust

Stefon Diggs, WR, Washington Commanders

Diggs can still shake coverage. It's on the tape. And he can catch touchdowns, too. Diggs, who has six scoring receptions on the season, now has a TD in three of his last four games. Diggs is also scoring 14.4 fantasy PPG during this stretch, averaging seven targets per game. While Diggs isn't an explosive playmaker at this stage of his career, he has the inside/outside alignment flexibility to gain positive matchups for quarterback Jayden Daniels, plus he is slippery after the catch. With some positive matchups looming (CIN, @ARI, @TEN), I like Diggs as a WR2/flex.

DJ Moore, WR, Buffalo Bills

Moore has been banged up this season, and he's missed time. However, in the five full games Moore has played, he's scored at least 12 fantasy points in four of them, with 16 or more in three. And the one game out of the five full Moore played where he didn't produce double-digit points came in a tough matchup against the Vikings' chaos-creating defense in Week 9. Moore has a touchdown grab in two of his last three games, with a total of three receptions of 20 or more yards during that stretch. Moore has two tougher upcoming matchups (MIA, KC), but as the top target for Josh Allen in Buffalo's explosive offense, he can be trusted as a WR2.

Harold Fannin Jr., TE, Cleveland Browns

The Browns are on a bye this week, but Fannin should be played in all formats going forward. Fannin, who was started in only 61.2% of ESPN leagues last week, has scored 16.2 fantasy PPG over his last four. And in the three games during that stretch with Deshaun Watson under center, Fannin had at least six targets and 90 yards receiving. Plus, the upcoming schedule, starting in Week 12, is positive (LV, CIN, ATL). Remember, with both Trey McBride and Brock Bowers now working with rookie quarterbacks, Fannin (who is currently TE4 in scoring) has a path to maintain his momentum and finish the season as a top-five tight end.

Parker Washington, WR, Jacksonville Jaguars

Washington's production hasn't been exactly steady this season (two games with fewer than five points, three with fewer than 15), and he has a catch rate of only 56.3%. However, Washington has scored 28 or more points in two of his last five games, with at least seven targets in four of five. And in coach Liam Coen's offense, the Jags can get Washington in positive one-on-ones, while also scheming open voids in zone coverage. Washington is an easy mover at the release, plus he can scoot after the catch. In this system, with Trevor Lawrence at quarterback, I'd trust Washington as higher-end WR2.

Jordyn Tyson, WR, New Orleans Saints

Tyson was active last week against the Panthers, only his second game as a pro after suffering a hamstring injury in camp. The rookie first-rounder caught 11 of 13 targets (both team highs), finishing with 80 yards on 32 routes run. Yes, Chris Olave is still the No. 1 option for the Saints, however, Tyson could continue to see more opportunities if teams roll coverage to Olave. Tyson has the high-level playmaking traits to potentially produce breakout weeks. He's a solid fit for coach Kellen Moore's route tree, and his upcoming schedule (@CHI, @CIN, GB, @CAR) could also lead to a heavy passing script for the Saints. Get him in the lineup as a flex.

Josh Downs, WR, Kansas City Chiefs

Patrick Mahomes is going to spread the ball around in Andy Reid's system, which caps the ceiling of his pass catchers. But if you are looking for a player to put in the WR3 or flex spot, Downs looks like a fit. Yes, we have only one game of tape with Downs in a Chiefs uniform (after he was traded from the Colts), but there are a lot of positives after watching him during last week's win over the Falcons. Downs scored 15.3 points, catching four of five targets for 53 yards (on only eight routes run) and a touchdown on a schemed wheel route. I would expect Downs' usage to climb quickly, as the Chiefs have some big-time upcoming matchups (ARI, @BUF, @LAR, @CIN), plus he has the route traits to uncover for Mahomes at multiple levels of the field.

Pass catchers not to trust

Jalen Coker, WR, Carolina Panthers

Coker started the season with a career-best 33.8 points in Week 1 versus the Bears, and he caught a total of 16 of 18 targets over his first two games. Since then, Coker has fewer than 10 points in five of seven games played, and he didn't record a reception (on four targets) in the Week 10 win over the Saints. With his low-level production in a struggling Panthers pass game, I can't trust Coker moving forward, despite his physical profile and route traits. He's a deeper-league WR3 at best at this point.

Tyler Warren, TE, Indianapolis Colts

I love the talent and skill set of Warren. That's why I had him ranked as a top-five tight end this summer. However, Warren's production has rapidly declined, as he's scored fewer than 10 fantasy points in three straight games (5.5 PPG). Plus, I don't understand his current route deployment. During this stretch, Warren has seen 20 targets, yet he's averaging only 5.4 air yards per target. He can press the seams, work the corner routes and more. Where is it? This Colts offense (after the trade deadline) has been a rough watch, and Warren's upcoming schedule is daunting (@HOU, @NYG, BYE, PHI). There's a reason he's falling in weekly rankings.

DK Metcalf, Pittsburgh Steelers

I've written about Metcalf before in this space, and not much has changed. Yes, Metcalf did score 15.4 fantasy points in the Sunday night loss to the Bengals, cashing in on a fourth quarter touchdown when the game was in control for Cincy. However, that was only Metcalf's second reception of the night, and he has fewer than 10 points in three of his last five games, despite seeing an average of 7.6 targets in each. With Aaron Rodgers also cooling off, I can't trust Metcalf as more than a boom/bust flex option moving forward.

Emeka Egbuka, WR, Tampa Bay Buccaneers

Egbuka was my guy this summer. I saw breakout potential, but it simply hasn't hit this season. Egbuka missed two games with an injury, and the Bucs have experienced disruption at quarterback due to Baker Mayfield's thumb injury -- and he is questionable again this week (foot). Egbuka (11.1 PPG) has scored fewer than 10 points in two of his last four games, and he has only two touchdown grabs on the season. Another thing working against Egbuka: this Tampa offense has attempted the fewest passes in the league (240). You can still play him, but he needs to remain as a flex option only.

A.J. Brown, WR, New England Patriots

Drake Maye (ankle) could be done for the season and Brown is dealing with yet another injury (hamstring). Brown has played in only four games for the Patriots (6.0 PPG), and he could miss more time. Without Maye, managers must downgrade the entire Patriots pass game with No. 2 Tommy DeVito in line to start in Week 12 versus the Chargers (after the team returns from the bye). When Brown is ready to return, he shouldn't be viewed as anything better than a WR3. It's been a tough year for the veteran receiver.

Expect less from these pass catchers

Trey McBride, TE, Arizona Cardinals

McBride is still a must-start, but it's fair to question whether he will continue to produce elite numbers with rookie Carson Beck now under center. In Beck's first NFL start this past Sunday, McBride scored a season-low 8.7 points in the loss to the Rams. Beck will go through some growing pains until he adjusts to pro speed/scheme, and that could impact McBride's numbers.

Deebo Samuel Sr., WR, San Francisco 49ers

Samuel scored a season-high 25.9 points in the Week 10 win over the Cowboys, catching three passes for 30 yards and a touchdown, plus he added 78 yards rushing (on three carries) and another score. Kyle Shanahan will continue to scheme touches for Samuel, as we saw on his 70-yard touchdown run against the poor Dallas defense, but with Mike Evans expected back and Keenan Allen joining the team via trade, Samuel can be used as nothing more than a touchdown-dependent WR3 or flex.

Deeper-league pass catchers to consider

Malachi Fields, WR, New York Giants (9.1% rostered)

Fields has scored 9.5 fantasy PPG over his last three, and he's averaging 4.7 targets during that stretch. With the aggressive throwing mentality of Giants quarterback J.J. McCarthy, Fields can make plays as a boundary option with his 6-foot-4, 222-pound frame.

Antonio Williams, WR, Washington Commanders (17.6% rostered)

Williams has scored 10 or more points in two of his last three games, and he's seen a total of 15 targets during this stretch. A savvy receiver with route traits and coverage awareness, Williams also caught a touchdown in last week's win over the Giants (his first since Week 1).

stories.headline: Historic usage rates are fueling Luka Doncic and the Lakers' offense
stories.summary: Doncic is pushing the boundaries of basketball production. But could that actually hurt the Lakers' title hopes?
stories.body:
Is there such a thing as too much Luka magic?

That question might seem blasphemous to Los Angeles Lakers fans savoring Luka Doncic's scorching start for the NBA's third-ranked offense, but it's one worth monitoring as he pushes the boundaries of basketball production.

Doncic has jumped to the front of the NBA MVP conversation by averaging 38.1 points per game, which would eclipse Michael Jordan for the highest scoring average since the 1976 NBA/ABA merger. But the Lakers guard is also posting a historic usage rate -- the percentage of his team's possessions he ends with a shot attempt, free throw attempt or turnover -- that sidles him with one of the heaviest offensive burdens in league history.

Given that ultra-high usage stars have always fallen short of winning a championship, should Doncic's heavy load start to raise alarm bells in Lakerland?

Los Angeles is tied for the league's best record at 13-3, largely because none of its opponents have effectively slowed down Doncic, who already has seven 40-point and two 50-point performances. The Lakers have a juicy plus-15.3 net rating when the Slovenian star is on the court and have already racked up seven double-digit victories.

L.A.'s extraordinary reliance on Doncic rekindles a debate about the perils of ball dominance. When one player is so responsible for his team's success, it leaves the roster exposed if he sustains an injury and increases the possibility the player might succumb to diminishing returns.

This is well-worn narrative territory that dates back decades:

Jordan needs to pass more. Allen Iverson can't do it by himself. Russell Westbrook is a ball hog.

Now, the Lakers' title aspirations will hinge on whether they can avoid some of the pitfalls that tripped up previous high-usage superstars.

Why Doncic faces a daunting precedent

The conditions are just right for Doncic to break calculators with his scoring and usage: The Lakers lost five of their top seven scorers from last season and don't ask any starting forwards to be major offensive contributors. At 27, Doncic is in his prime, has worked his way into excellent shape and is seemingly on a mission to make the most of his new status as the face of the post-LeBron James Lakers.

"[Doncic excels because of] the volume of the three-point shot combined with his ability to get to the free throw line," Lakers coach JJ Redick said Wednesday. "If you look at most elite scorers, it's a tale as old as time. Jordan, Kobe [Bryant], they got to the free throw line. It's that, and when you're shooting 12 or 13 shots a game at 40 percent from three, you can really score at volume."

As a result, Doncic's early work has been off the charts.

This graphic shows the scoring and usage rate for the 285 players who have logged the most minutes during the 2026-27 season. Doncic sits all alone in the upper right corner with a significant gap between himself and a tier of A-list stars that includes Shai Gilgeous-Alexander, Victor Wembanyama, Stephen Curry and Giannis Antetokounmpo.

Doncic's 40.4 usage rate is currently the third-highest mark since tracking began in 1967, trailing only Westbrook's 41.7 on the 2016-17 Oklahoma City Thunder and James Harden's 40.5 on the 2018-19 Houston Rockets.

While Doncic's usage represents a career high, his performance this season is an extension of his preferred play style, not a radical one-off experiment. In fact, Doncic's 37.6 usage on the 2022-23 Dallas Mavericks and his 38.1 usage for last year's Lakers are among the top 10 marks ever posted.

Here's a splash of cold water: While 41 players have posted a usage rate above 35.0 for a season, none won a championship that year. This group includes Hall of Famers such as Jordan, Iverson, Bryant and Dwyane Wade, plus future Hall of Famers such as Harden, Westbrook, Antetokounmpo and Joel Embiid.

The explanation is straightforward: It's easier to win championships with multiple stars and reliable supporting scorers, and it's more difficult and less sensible for one player to completely dominate his team's offense when he's playing with another star or stars.

Jordan is the quintessential example. His Chicago Bulls were swept in the first round by the Boston Celtics when his usage peaked at 38.3 in 1986-87; but Scottie Pippen's growth, the supporting cast's development and some coaxing from coach Phil Jackson brought Jordan's usage rate down to a more reasonable baseline throughout the 1990s. During each of Chicago's six championship seasons, Jordan still led the league in scoring, but his usage ranged from 31.7 to 34.7.

Similar circumstances shaped the championship years of Bryant and James.

Bryant's usage peaked at 38.7 in 2005-06, when the Lakers lost to the Phoenix Suns in the first round. Once Los Angeles reloaded with Pau Gasol and Lamar Odom, Bryant's usage landed at 32.2 and 32.3 during the 2008-09 and 2009-10 championship seasons.

James posted a career-high 33.8 usage for the 2008-09 Cleveland Cavaliers, who lost to the Orlando Magic in the Eastern Conference finals. During his four championship seasons, James' usage landed between 30.2 and 32.0 as he enjoyed successful pairings with Wade, Kyrie Irving and Anthony Davis.

Doncic vs. the two MVPs of usage rate

While Doncic is still seeking his first championship, his career has told a similar "less is more" story.

In 2025-26, his highest-usage season to date (38.1), Doncic suffered a hamstring injury in April that sidelined him for the Lakers' entire postseason. In 2022-23, his next-highest-usage season (37.6), the Mavericks endured a late-season collapse and didn't reach the playoffs.

By contrast, Doncic's deepest playoff run -- a 2024 NBA Finals appearance with the Mavericks -- came in his fifth-highest-usage season (36.0). Though his role narrowed slightly in his first full season playing with Irving, Doncic was nevertheless worn down by the end of the five-game Finals loss to the Celtics.

The Lakers' 109-97 loss to the lowly Utah Jazz on Wednesday provided a glimpse of what can go wrong when Doncic isn't firing on all cylinders. With Doncic scoring 29 points on 10-for-28 shooting and Austin Reaves sidelined with a heel injury on the second night of a back-to-back, the Lakers were held under 100 points for just the second time this season.

"The shot creation that is required from [Doncic] takes its toll," Redick said after Wednesday's loss.

Given that Doncic's current usage rate is hovering above 40, let's look back at what happened when Westbrook and Harden exceeded that threshold.

Westbrook's 2016-17 campaign with Oklahoma City shares some similarities with Doncic's current season. The polarizing All-Star guard was free to cook after Kevin Durant departed for the Golden State Warriors in free agency, much like Doncic's new reality following James' summer exit to the Philadelphia 76ers. That season, Westbrook led the NBA in scoring, won his only MVP award and captained a 47-win team. All those accolades are in reach for Doncic this season.

Yet there are some key differences between the two players: Doncic's 64.4 true shooting percentage this season is much better than Westbrook's 55.4 true shooting percentage in his MVP campaign, and the Lakers' offense is much more efficient than the 2016-17 Thunder's attack, which ranked 15th despite Westbrook's career campaign.

When the Thunder fell to Houston in five games in the first round of the 2017 playoffs, there was little doubt that their offense suffered from an unhealthy balance. In a memorable Game 2, Westbrook scored 51 points and attempted 43 shots, but OKC still lost. That season is remembered as a cautionary tale: A one-man offense, no matter how determined the man is, will struggle in the playoffs.

Harden's 2018-19 season is more comparable to Doncic's current run. That season, Harden averaged a career-high 36.1 points and captained a 53-win squad. Harden's true shooting percentage that season was 61.6 -- close to Doncic's current number -- and Houston boasted the NBA's second-best offense.

That Rockets team had a legitimate chance to win the title, but it ultimately lost a second-round series against the defending champion Warriors in six games. Harden and Chris Paul couldn't overcome Golden State's talent and experience, even though Durant was sidelined for the series finale with a calf injury.

Despite their success, the Rockets' 2018-19 campaign also is remembered as a cautionary tale: After the loss to the Warriors, Harden and Paul reportedly clashed over the lack of ball movement and heavy reliance on isolation sets. The Rockets traded Paul before the next season.

Can Doncic be the one? A recent champion offers hope

There is one relevant data point working in Doncic and the Lakers' favor.

Gilgeous-Alexander led the Thunder to the 2025 title with a 34.8 usage rate, the highest mark for a championship-winning player since tracking began in 1967.

As analytics have helped refine modern offenses, many teams have decided to empower their best players. More than half of the top 50 usage seasons since 1967 have occurred in the past decade, and Doncic's remarkable start can be viewed as the purest example.

NBA teams have also gotten more sophisticated in measuring workload with advancements in player tracking data.

"I don't believe in usage rate," Redick said Wednesday. "True usage rate is a better approximation, that's time on ball. [Doncic] has really bought into playing more off the ball, and he also just generates points for us.

"You have to factor in all the potential assists we get with him having the ball in his hands and coming off actions. [His usage rate] is not a concern."

By Redick's preferred definition, Doncic is more in line with his fellow stars. Through Tuesday, he ranks fourth leaguewide with 9.4 minutes of possession per game.

If Gilgeous-Alexander and the Thunder successfully pushed the usage boundary two years ago, can a closely monitored Doncic push it even further this season?

That's a fair question. But don't forget that Oklahoma City possessed the NBA's best defense in 2024-25 and Jalen Williams was a very strong secondary option in the postseason. Even so, the heavily favored Thunder barely outlasted the Indiana Pacers in seven games because Gilgeous-Alexander's scoring volume and efficiency dipped noticeably by the end of the playoffs.

While the 2026-27 Lakers don't possess a 2025 Thunder-like defense, they do have some structural and stylistic advantages that could help Doncic fare better than Westbrook and Harden.

Most importantly, Los Angeles has a proven secondary scorer and playmaker in Reaves, who is averaging 24.7 points and 4.7 assists in pursuit of his first All-Star selection. Westbrook's oft-overlooked sidekick in 2016-17 was Victor Oladipo, who averaged 15.9 points and 2.6 assists. Paul averaged 15.6 points and 8.2 assists as Houston's second option in 2018-19, but he and Harden often operated in my-turn, your-turn fashion before their partnership dissolved.

Doncic and Reaves appear to be more natural stylistic counterparts, and they haven't exhibited any interpersonal tension.

Pace is another potential advantage for the Lakers as compared with Harden's Rockets. Houston ranked 27th in pace in 2018-19, slowing the game down so that Harden could attack his man with an array of one-on-one moves or force double-teams that would create open 3-pointers for his supporting cast.

The Lakers rank in the middle of the pack by pace this season, and Doncic leads a more free-flowing attack that has generated lots of transition opportunities. Keeping the entire team involved and invested is crucial to winning when one player controls as much of the action as Doncic.

But the Lakers' hopes are highly leveraged on the health and productivity of Doncic and Reaves. They will always welcome consistent scoring contributions from center Walker Kessler and the likes of Quentin Grimes, who poured in a career-high 47 points in an overtime win over the Charlotte Hornets on Tuesday.

Nobody was happier to see that breakthrough performance than Doncic, who repeatedly overruled Redick's playcalls to force-feed the veteran guard down the stretch.

"[Grimes] got it going and he brought us back in the game," Doncic said. "We tried to give him the ball as he deserved. What an amazing game."

Doncic is bound to face questions about his durability and fitness until he breaks through for his first championship. But his passing ability and willingness to spread the wealth are among the best reasons to believe he and the Lakers can defy the challenging history of high-usage stars.

stories.headline: Skubal to ...? What about other big free agents? How MLB offseason dominoes fall
stories.summary: Based on what ESPN's Jeff Passan is hearing, we predict where the top names available will land -- and how they impact each other.
stories.body:
The countdown to the impending lockout is getting closer, which means the MLB offseason will likely grind to a depressing halt when the clock hits midnight on Dec. 1. Until then, teams are continuing to act like it's business as usual -- Jake Bauers to the Boston Red Sox, Dustin May to the Chicago White Sox and Evan Phillips to the Atlanta Braves have been the most significant free agent signings so far.

The big prize in a weak class is two-time Cy Young winner Tarik Skubal -- and he's expected to sign before the sport shuts down. This happened prior to the last lockout following the 2021 season, when Corey Seager, Marcus Semien, Javier Baez, Max Scherzer, Robbie Ray and Kevin Gausman all signed $100 million-plus contracts before the lockout went into effect.

Skubal might be the only nine-figure free agent this year, but the ripple effect of where he lands will dictate the offseason.

Using Jeff Passan's intel on what he's hearing will happen over the next two weeks as a guideline, let's kick off this offseason edition of dominoes with Skubal going ... East?

Tarik Skubal to New York Mets

The Mets are the favorite to land Skubal, according to Passan, in part because of the Los Angeles Dodgers' desire for a shorter-term commitment. Of course, Skubal loved his time with L.A. and lives in Arizona in the offseason, so maybe the Dodgers will view this as a situation of "sign him while you can" and eventually give Skubal whatever it takes.

If the labor negotiations do eventually end up with some sort of capped system, this could be the last chance for the Dodgers to empty their bank vault for several years. Their primary need for their long-term future -- regardless of payroll rules -- is getting younger in the lineup (Andy Pages was the only regular younger than 30 years old) rather than adding more starting pitching. Instead of locking up another starter, they might be eyeing the free agent class following the 2029 season for their next big signing: Elly De La Cruz, Brice Turang, Jordan Walker and, if they want to dip into pitching, Paul Skenes.

Enter the Mets, a big-market team with money to spend while the rules permit, holes in the rotation to fill and losing ways to mend. They have two young rotation anchors in Nolan McLean and Christian Scott, but some of their veteran additions haven't worked out, including last offseason's trade for Freddy Peralta or Sean Manaea's three-year deal two years ago. The Mets haven't had a pitcher finish in the top five of the Cy Young voting since Jacob deGrom in 2020; they need Skubal more than the Dodgers need him.

Michael King to San Diego Padres

The Padres' new owners appear willing to keep up the spending habits of the late Peter Seidler, so that's the good news. The bad news is they need to fill at least three-fifths of a rotation, with King, Walker Buehler, Robbie Ray, Casey Mize and Nick Pivetta all free agents (Randy Vasquez is the lone holdover and they're hoping for a comeback from Joe Musgrove, who returned in the postseason after missing two full seasons). Swiping Skubal from the Dodgers would be a double whammy -- helping yourselves while hurting your enemy -- but logic says the Padres need to spread the money around. Re-signing King, who has a 3.15 ERA in his three years in San Diego, should be the first step.

Trevor Rogers to Toronto Blue Jays

Are the Blue Jays interested in Skubal or are they interested in rotation help in general? Because after finishing last in the majors in runs scored, they definitely need to boost the lineup. Bottom line: After dropping to 79-83 in 2026, the Jays need to add an impact player or two no matter the position.

That might be Rogers, who ranks fifth among starting pitchers on ESPN's ranking of the top 50 free agents -- behind Skubal, Peralta, Japanese right-hander Kaima Taira and King -- but he might be the best combination of age (he's entering his age-29 season) and upside (3.16 ERA over the past two seasons).

Rogers isn't overpowering, but he possesses a five-pitch mix and induces a ton of chase while issuing just 39 walks in 30 starts for the Baltimore Orioles this past season. He does have some injury history -- missing most of 2023 with biceps and shoulder issues, and he had a knee injury at the start of 2025 -- but that also means he doesn't have a lot of wear on his left arm. The Blue Jays are dreaming of a Skubal/Dylan Cease combo, but Cease, Rogers, Jose Soriano and Trey Yesavage would rank as one of the top foursomes in the majors -- and there could still be room left to sign a hitter.

The one issue with Rogers is that he declined the qualifying offer the Orioles gave him, so the Blue Jays would lose their second- and fifth-highest draft picks as well as forfeit $1 million from their international pool money. Losing those picks will cool some teams on Rogers, but the Blue Jays, after coming so close in 2025, are determined to get back to the World Series.

Freddy Peralta to Baltimore Orioles

That leaves Peralta as the next pitcher in line. The Orioles "are everywhere," Passan reported, and have a willingness to carry a top-10 payroll -- which, according to Cot's Contracts, they last reached in 2005 (they were 14th in 2026). The Orioles were 17th in rotation ERA and face the prospect of losing Rogers, so they will be looking for a starter to join Shane Baz and Kyle Bradish to lead the rotation. This could be a best-case scenario: Rogers turned down the qualifying offer, so if he signs for more than $50 million with another team, the Orioles receive a draft pick at the end of the first round. Since Peralta was traded during his free agent season, he can be signed without any penalty.

Kaima Taira (and Clay Holmes) to Chicago Cubs

We know the Cubs need major help in terms of starting pitching -- they basically need to fill an entire rotation. Re-signing Holmes is a popular prediction, but they'll need more than him. The Cubs haven't signed a pitcher to a nine-figure deal since Yu Darvish in 2018, so that takes them out of the Skubal sweepstakes and perhaps Peralta as well, given his projected contract of four years, $96 million. They prefer not to sign free agents with qualifying offers, so that is likely to eliminate Rogers. The highest-ranked remaining starter would be the 5-foot-8 Taira, who had a 1.36 ERA in Japan in 2026.

Chicago went the Japan route three years and got three solid years from Shota Imanaga, but Taira has better stuff and shouldn't be as prone to the home run. His projected contract is five years for $72.5 million.

Randy Arozarena to Philadelphia Phillies

Let's move away from the pitching market to a big-market team looking to make a major signing. The Phillies need a hitter. Preferably right-handed. Preferably an outfielder. Preferably a good defender to help one of the more porous defenses in the majors. Perhaps someone who reportedly prefers to head back to the East Coast.

Passan reports that teams are balking at Arozarena's $100 million asking price, but with an aging roster that needs to win now, the Phillies might be the one team willing to get close to nine figures -- after all, president of baseball operations Dave Dombrowski isn't one to shy away from paying to get the guy he wants.

Arozarena had an outstanding under-the-radar season in Seattle in 2026, posting 5.7 WAR and leading the American League in runs scored despite playing in a tough hitters' park with a bad lineup around him. He's gone 20/20 all six of his full seasons in the majors and has been extremely durable, averaging 154 games over the past five seasons. He's a below-average defender in left field, but, hey, when do the Phillies care about defense anyway?

Seiya Suzuki to San Diego Padres

With Arozarena heading to the Phillies in our scenario, Suzuki is the next domino to fall ... going to San Diego. Besides their need for starting pitchers, the Padres have also been considering some of the bigger hitters, with Passan labeling the Padres the favorites to land Suzuki -- although, he also makes sense for the Seattle Mariners or returning to the Cubs.

Suzuki is coming off a .270/.368/.473 season with Chicago while posting the best defensive metrics of his career (88th percentile in outs above average and 94th percentile in arm value). A projected four-year, $90 million contract is steep for a player entering his age-32 season, but the Padres' window is closing the older Manny Machado and Xander Bogaerts get (with years to go on each of their contracts). The Padres would play Suzuki in right field and move Fernando Tatis Jr. back to the infield, probably second base, where he started 50 games last season.

Jazz Chisholm Jr. to Toronto Blue Jays

After signing Rogers, the Blue Jays still have work to do. Arozarena and Suzuki are possibilities, but Chisholm, with a two-year, $46 million projection, is a less expensive and younger option. While the Yankees seem content to let him walk after inconsistent results at the plate and lack of focus, Chisholm has averaged 2.9 WAR over each of the past three seasons and is an excellent defender at second base (at least via Statcast). He was worth 4.1 WAR in 2025, when he hit 31 home runs, but fell off to 1.7 in 2026. The Jays could turn Ernie Clement back into a super utility guy to play Chisholm at second base, plus Chisholm has the ability to shift into the outfield as needed.

Brandon Lowe to New York Yankees

With David Bednar accepting the Yankees' qualifying offer, general manager Brian Cashman can breathe a little easier about his bullpen and turn his attention to replacing Chisholm at second. Maybe Anthony Volpe is the guy. Or, after more than 2,000 plate appearances in the majors with an OPS+ of 83, maybe he's not. Lowe is a big upgrade in power -- he has hit 66 home runs over the past two seasons -- and played the best defense of his career after changing his pre-pitch routine. While it would be wonderful to see the Pittsburgh Pirates re-sign Lowe, his projected four-year, $80 million contract is more likely to place him in the Bronx than next to the Roberto Clemente Bridge.

Teruaki Sato to Los Angeles Angels

It will be fascinating to see what kind of deal the Japanese slugger lands. He looks a lot like Munetaka Murakami did a year ago, and Murakami had to settle for a lower-than-expected two-year, $34 million contract with the White Sox. He hit .207 for them this past season, but with 35 home runs and a ton of walks and strikeouts. The overall offensive package was productive, although Murakami hit .156 the final two months. It's hard to say how those results will affect the evaluations of Sato.

Sato was primarily a third baseman in Japan; if he can stay there, he could end up with the Phillies -- or the Yankees, except we have Lowe going to New York -- but most believe he'll end up in left field or first base. Maybe, like Murakami, Sato ends up in a surprise destination. The Angels were 28th in the majors in OPS at third base and need to take a risk to boost the offense. If Sato's defensive chops aren't up to par at third base, they can try him in left field.

Adrian Morejon to Los Angeles Dodgers

Where does this leave the Dodgers? There are other good starting pitchers out there: Tyler Mahle, Nick Martinez, Gausman, Imanaga, Foster Griffin. Given that May's deal with the White Sox is for three years and $52.5 million, much higher than expected, we'll see if the market now explodes for this group. The Braves, San Francisco Giants and Houston Astros are among the teams in the mix here, along with the Cubs and Padres. The Tampa Bay Rays will need to re-sign Martinez or replace him. Luis Arraez and Ian Happ are the other top position players.

None of those players feel like a fit for the Dodgers. Morejon, however, is one of the top relievers in the game. The Dodgers already lost Phillips, and Alex Vesia is also a free agent, so they could use a high-leverage reliever -- yes, even though Edwin Diaz and Tanner Scott are already two of the game's highest-paid relievers and signed for two more seasons.

Again, the rules might be changing. This could be one last chance for the Dodgers to play Moneyball.

stories.headline: NHL Tonight: Guide to all 12 games on another packed Thursday
stories.summary: Find game previews, betting intel, broadcast information, stats and highlights here.
stories.body:
It's Thursday, which means there is a packed schedule of NHL action.

Among the 12 games on the docket, there's a 2026 Eastern Conference finals rematch, a very legit potential Stanley Cup Final preview, and a rematch of Stars-Golden Knights after the clubs' overtime thriller on Tuesday.

But be forewarned! There are zero NHL games on Friday, so enjoy tonight instead.

Read on for a look at what you need to know for each game, including betting info and broadcast details.

Odds are provided by DraftKings and subject to change.

Los Angeles Kings at Toronto Maple Leafs

7 p.m. ET (ESPN+) | TOR -110, O/U: 6.5

Jim Hiller revenge game?

The current Maple Leafs head coach was fired from the same role by the Kings this past spring, so perhaps he'll use his inside information to help his current team earn a long-awaited win.

Toronto has lost seven straight games, and six straight at Scotiabank Arena. L.A. has not exactly been lighting the league on fire, but the Kings enter this contest having beaten the Bruins 3-0 in Boston on Tuesday.

The Leafs are led across the scoring board this season by Auston Matthews, who has 12 goals and 18 assists. The Kings are similarly led by Artemi Panarin (eight goals, 11 assists), though he has missed the past two games for personal reasons and his status for Thursday is unclear.

Philadelphia Flyers at Ottawa Senators

7 p.m. ET (ESPN+) | OTT -175, O/U: 5.5

By a quirk of the 2026-27 NHL schedule, this is the final time that these two teams will play in the regular season. The home team has won each game in the series so far -- 2-1 Senators on Oct. 8 and 3-1 Flyers on Oct. 17.

From an overall perspective, the Senators have to feel quite a bit better about their season thus far (second in the Atlantic Division with 30 points) than the Flyers (sixth in the Metro with 20). However, Philly has won three of its last five games (sandwiched around a pair of losses to the Oilers).

Tim Stutzle leads Ottawa across the board in scoring with 11 goals and 15 assists, while Matvei Michkov has the Flyers' goals lead (11) and Trevor Zegras leads in helpers (10).

The real disparity is in goal, where Linus Ullmark leads the league in both goals-against average (1.42) and save percentage (.940), while Philly netminders Dan Vladar and Joseph Woll have combined for a 3.29 GAA and .887 SV%.

St. Louis Blues at Pittsburgh Penguins

7 p.m. ET (ESPN+) | PIT -112, O/U: 6.5

On the face of things, this is just a mid-November game between two seventh-place teams. But pull back a layer, and perhaps there's some early trade deadline speculation to be had?

From all reports, the Penguins' big three of Sidney Crosby, Evgeni Malkin and Kris Letang aren't going anywhere. But pending free agent Erik Karlsson -- who leads the team in points, and has yet to win a Stanley Cup -- seems like the kind of player a contender might covet.

Likewise, for the teams in need of a veteran goalie to boost their tandem, Jordan Binnington has clearly been usurped as the Blues' No. 1 by Joel Hofer, but he is the man who backstopped the franchise to a Cup in 2019, and Team Canada to the gold medal game in the 2026 Olympics.

Buffalo Sabres at Washington Capitals

7 p.m. ET (ESPN+) | WSH -142, O/U: 6.5

Last season, Alex Tuch was with the Sabres, and helped them end the league's longest playoff drought.

This season, he's leading the Capitals in goals (12), while the Sabres can't seem to find the right formula to string wins together (and have lost their last five).

Thursday's game is the second one pitting Tuch against his former teammates, although the return contest in Buffalo won't take place until March 18. In the first matchup between the clubs this season, the Caps won 4-3 in OT -- with Tuch scoring the game-winner 3:42 into the extra session, of course.

Montreal Canadiens at Carolina Hurricanes

7 p.m. ET (ESPN+) | CAR -265, O/U: 6.5

This past spring, the Hurricanes lost only three total games en route to winning the Stanley Cup. One of them was to the Canadiens in the Eastern Conference finals, and this will be their second matchup of the regular season.

The Canes come into this game razor-hot, as winners of four straight -- and having returned from playing two games in Finland, the ancestral home of saunas. In fact, they've won eight of their last nine, although some of the competition during that span was not exactly top-tier.

Montreal has lost two straight, but beat the rival Bruins in Boston and took the juggernaut Wild to OT.

Carolina's Taylor Hall and Montreal's Zack Bolduc each had a pair of goals in that earlier contest; is there another big night in store on Thursday?

New York Islanders at Winnipeg Jets

7 p.m. ET (ESPN+) | WPG -125, O/U: 5.5

The Isles bring a three-game winning streak to Manitoba, taking on the Jets, whose recent streak of Ws ended at six.

New York is fourth in the Metro with 24 points, while the Jets are sixth in the Central with 23; both teams are right in the wild-card mix in their respective conferences.

This is the first of two games between the teams this season, the other taking place on Long Island the day after American Thanksgiving.

So what to expect? Lots of goals, apparently! The Jets won both games last season (5-2 on Oct. 13 and 5-4 on Jan. 13).

Edmonton Oilers at Tampa Bay Lightning

7:30 p.m. ET (Disney+/ESPN+/Hulu) | TB -142, O/U: 6.5

Can I interest you in a game featuring three perennial Hart Trophy candidates -- playing for teams that could very well meet again in the Cup Final in June?

Connor McDavid's exploits have been well-covered here and elsewhere, but his quest for 200 points continues. Right by his side is Leon Draisaitl, who is second in the league in scoring.

On the other side, Nikita Kucherov -- the reigning MVP -- is tied for seventh in scoring, with 30 points, still putting up big numbers after declaring that that he won't re-sign with the Lightning this coming offseason.

One other fun factor here: the Oilers are 10-0-1 on the road this season, the only NHL team without a regulation loss. The Lightning are 9-1-0 at home, tying the 2020-21 season for their best start at home in a season, according to ESPN Research. Which side blinks first?

Columbus Blue Jackets at Chicago Blackhawks

8 p.m. ET (ESPN+) | CBJ -166, O/U: 5.5

Well, they can't all be matchups between potential Cup Finalists can they?

Nevertheless, these teams have been two of the most generous in the NHL this season in terms of goals allowed per game -- 3.32 for Columbus, 4.05 for Chicago -- so maybe we'll get an offensive onslaught.

Unfortunately, Connor Bedard is day-to-day after sustaining a shoulder injury on Tuesday, but the Blue Jackets should have leading goal-scorer Kent Johnson and leading assist man Zach Werenski in the lineup.

Minnesota Wild at Calgary Flames

8 p.m. ET (ESPN+) | MIN -205, O/U: 6.5

Typically when one of the NHL's top contenders plays against a club that has fully embraced a rebuild/retool era, the contender wins -- by a lot. But the first game between these clubs ended with the scoreboard reading Flames 2, Wild 1.

That game was a Devin Cooley special, as the most interesting man in hockey made 38 saves, while Aydar Suniev and Joel Farabee provided just enough offense to earn the W.

The numbers would certainly indicate that Minnesota should win this one, but we'll see what happens when the proverbial fur starts flying in Calgary!

Anaheim Ducks at Colorado Avalanche

9 p.m. ET (ESPN+) | COL -155, O/U: 6.5

Whether or not the Ducks win, every game is officially a must-watch because of Cutter Gauthier.

The 22-year-old -- with indisputably one of the best names in pro sports -- became the first NHL player ever to record four hat tricks in a single month, scoring three against the Blues on Tuesday (the Ducks lost, but oh well).

This will be the first matchup of the season pitting these two teams, after both made the playoffs last season. As the Ducks enjoy the Gauthier breakout, the Avs will continue to be without superstars Nathan MacKinnon and Cale Makar. Who steps up to make up for their absence?

Vancouver Canucks at Seattle Kraken

9:40 p.m. ET (ESPN+) | SEA -192, O/U: 6.5

At some point down the road, this is going to be an epic and meaningful rivalry, with each game pivotal as the Canucks and Kraken clash with playoff dreams on the line.

We're not quite at that point yet. The Canucks are eighth in the Pacific, at 5-17-1, while the Kraken are sixth, at 9-8-1.

However, two of those wins for Vancouver came in the past two games -- is there a winning streak on the way? Seattle's playoff hopes -- such as they are -- will take a big blow if the Canucks earn a third here.

Dallas Stars at Vegas Golden Knights

10 p.m. ET (Disney+/ESPN+/Hulu) | VGK -125, O/U: 5.5

Sometimes one tunes into an NHL game and witnesses a superb individual or team performance, setting records or achieving milestones.

Other times, it's just an instant classic thriller with high entertainment value.

Such was the case for these two teams in their contest on Tuesday, a 4-3 OT win for the Stars after trailing 3-1 with as little as 1:21 left of the third. Mikko Rantanen scored the equalizer with just five seconds remaining before Miro Heiskanen netted the game-winner 3:36 into the extra session.

The stakes remain high in this one. Vegas is second in the Pacific behind Edmonton, trailing the Oilers by seven points with both having played 23 games. Dallas is second in the Central, down eight points to Minnesota (but in two fewer games played).

Oh, and if the scores aren't entirely settled after this showdown, the two teams meet again on Feb. 20 in the Stadium Series at AT&T Stadium.

Reminder: Fans can catch all the action in the NHL streaming hub and on the ESPN App.

With news on Wednesday that Boston College will be retiring Johnny Gaudreau's number, memorable jersey retirements are on the mind of hockey fans. And there was a particularly notable one on this date in history.

On Nov. 19, 1997, the Pittsburgh Penguins retired Mario Lemieux's No. 66. Lemieux had retired following Pittsburgh's elimination in the 1997 Stanley Cup playoffs, and the Hockey Hall of Fame waived its usual three-year waiting period to induct him months afterwards. So after his induction on Nov. 17, the Penguins held their ceremony two days later.

Unlike other jersey retirements, Lemieux's No. 66 was worn again... by Mario himself, after he unretired on Dec. 27, 2000. He would wear that number until he retired for good on Jan. 24, 2006 (during Sidney Crosby's rookie season).

stories.headline: Max Verstappen rejects F1's new biometric health plan for 'privacy' reasons
stories.summary: Max Verstappen has said he will not give permission to Formula 1 and its new partner Whoop to broadcast his biometric data during races.
stories.body:
Max Verstappen has said he will not give permission to Formula 1 and its new partner Whoop to broadcast his biometric data during races.

On Wednesday, F1 announced a new commercial partnership with fitness wearable company Whoop, including plans to incorporate biometric data from drivers in its future broadcasts.

Whoop devices have the potential to monitor the physiological metrics of the wearer, such as heart rate, respiratory rate, blood oxygen level, skin temperature, sleep patterns, and stress.

According to an F1 press release, "a cornerstone of the partnership will be the development of new broadcast storytelling experiences, featuring select insights delivered in the right way in collaboration with the drivers to provide fans with a real-time window into the physical realities of racing."

Due to the personal nature of the data collected by a Whoop device, F1 would need permission from drivers to broadcast it.

Verstappen said he would not be willing to participate in the project and revealed he does not even monitor his own heart rate while training.

"I won't be involved," Verstappen was quoted as saying by Motorsport.com. "I don't use any device, also not for my training, I don't use anything. First of all, I don't like to be tracked and I know when I'm tired.

"If other drivers want to [share], then sure. But for me, it's not something that I like and also not something that I want people to see or that I want to show."

Asked if his decision was due to privacy, he added: "Yes, also that. People don't need to know my heart rate. I also don't want to know my heart rate! I know when it's high and I know when it's low.

"For me, it's definitely a privacy thing, but, as I said, I also don't use it privately for training either."

- Lando Norris, Max Verstappen confident in F1's decision to race in Middle East

- Max Verstappen: I don't need Kimi Antonelli to motivate me to stay in F1

- Valtteri Bottas to race for Cadillac in 2027 after Colton Herta 'noise'

The use of heart rate monitoring during races is not entirely new in motor racing and was debuted in F1's feeder series, Formula 2, in 2023.

F1 CEO Stefano Domenicali said he was hopeful the Whoop partnership will add a new dimension for fans following race broadcasts.

"For the first time we'll be able to bring fans even closer to understanding what some of our drivers experience physically and mentally during the most intense moments of a race," Domenicali said. "The opportunity to uncover new insights, tell new stories and showcase the world-class athleticism that goes into making F1 one of the most extreme and exciting sports in the world, is truly groundbreaking.

"I can't wait to see these insights come to life through our broadcasts, giving fans a completely new way to experience Formula 1 while highlighting the incredible strength, resilience, and determination required to compete at the highest level of motorsport."

stories.headline: Kayla Harrison, Amanda Nunes reclaim leading roles in women's P4P top 10
stories.summary: Who do Kayla Harrison and Amanda Nunes replace in ESPN's P4P women's top 10?
stories.body:
Hello (again), Kayla Harrison and Amanda Nunes. Goodbye (for now), Valentina Shevchenko and Zhang Weili. The top of the ESPN women's MMA pound-for-pound rankings has a new look.

Harrison and Nunes, both of whom had been ineligible for the top 10 because of inactivity, returned over the weekend for a clash of elites at UFC 334. Harrison, defending her bantamweight championship for the first time after nearly a year and a half out of the cage while healing from surgery for herniated discs in her neck, scored a fourth-round submission of Nunes, who had been retired for nearly 3½ years. As a result, Harrison takes over the No. 1 ranking and Nunes, a former two-division champion and the consensus GOAT of women's MMA, is No. 2.

The former occupants of those spots, Shevchenko and Zhang, are newly ineligible for the rankings because it's been over a year since they have fought and they have nothing scheduled. Those two former champions drop out, and the rest of the women's top 10 remains the same.

In the men's rankings, UFC heavyweight champion Ciryl Gane moves up one spot to No. 7 on the strength of his decision win over Josh Hokit in their title bout at UFC 334.

For the ESPN divisional MMA rankings, click here.

Note: Results are current; rankings are as of Nov. 18. To be eligible for the rankings, a fighter must have competed over the past 12 months or must have an upcoming fight booked. Fighters who have been dropped for inactivity can be reinstated only after they compete.

Women's pound-for-pound rankings

1. Kayla Harrison

UFC bantamweight champion

Previous ranking: Unranked

Record: 20-1

Last: W (Sub4) vs. Amanda Nunes, Nov. 14

Next: TBA

Harrison stepped into the Octagon at UFC 334 already a reigning champion, but her submission win over Nunes was truly her crowning achievement. The backstory about their shared training gym history added drama to the buildup, but what mattered most about this matchup was that Harrison, who had voiced her goal to be the greatest ever in women's MMA, was facing the woman who has lived up to that standard. After choking out Nunes, what can Harrison do for an encore? Can any other woman in the sport give her a fight? Maybe it won't come to that. Harrison and Nunes both called for a rematch -- but at featherweight. That would lessen Harrison's burden in dealing with her toughest foe: the weigh-in scale.

2. Amanda Nunes

UFC bantamweight

Previous ranking: Unranked

Record: 23-6

Last: L (Sub4) vs. Kayla Harrison, Nov. 14

Next: TBA

Nunes' return from retirement did not go as she had hoped, but her failing was not so much about deteriorated physical abilities as it was about her ill-advised choice to venture too much into the grappling wheelhouse of Harrison, a two-time Olympic judo gold medalist. If Nunes gets the rematch both women are calling for, but this time at 145 pounds, that would seem to be to the advantage of Harrison, the bigger woman. But a redo would give Nunes another opportunity to lean into her own prodigious strength as a striker.

3. Cris Cyborg

PFL featherweight champion

Record: 30-2, 1 NC

Last: W (UD) vs. Ketlen Vieira, Aug. 22

Next: TBA

It had been a while since Cyborg had fought an elite opponent in MMA until she met Larissa Pacheco in 2024. That was a legitimate matchup -- and many within the industry were predicting Cyborg's downfall. Instead, she took out the PFL's two-weight champion, upending all of Pacheco's momentum. One of the original pioneers of women's MMA is once again a champion after getting her second career submission at PFL Lyon in December. The PFL promoted her fight with Vieira as a retirement bout, but after her win Cyborg did not sound like someone who is done fighting.

4. Natalia Silva

UFC flyweight champion

Record: 21-5-1

Last: W (UD) vs. Wang Cong, Oct. 3

Next: TBA

Silva was looking every bit the part of a future UFC champion following a dominant display against Alexa Grasso at UFC 315 and a victory over Rose Namajunas at UFC 324. And now she has fulfilled that expectation, beating Wang at UFC 332 to win the belt vacated by injured Valentina Shevchenko. Silva's stick-and-move style has frustrated even the highest level of opponent, and she's got youth on her side as she won't turn 30 until 2027.

5. Mackenzie Dern

UFC strawweight champion

Record: 17-5

Last: W (UD) vs. Gillian Robertson, Aug. 15

Next: TBA

Dern's rise to the 115-pound throne was truly a changing of the guard. She is the division's first first-time champion since 2019, because the previous three champs -- Zhang Weili, Carla Esparza and Rose Namajunas -- all were in their second reigns. Dern, nearly a decade into her MMA career after multiple jiu-jitsu world championships, has won four fights in a row, including a dominant performance against a fellow grappling-heavy fighter, Robertson, in her first title defense.

6. Alexa Grasso

UFC flyweight

Record: 18-5-1

Last: W (UD) vs. Manon Fiorot, Sept. 12

Next: TBA

Grasso went nearly three years without winning a fight, but her 2023 win right before the skid was a huge one, a submission of Valentina Shevchenko for the UFC title. What followed were two more fights with Shevchenko -- a draw, then a loss -- and then a loss to Natalia Silva. But she reasserted herself with a finish of Maycee Barber in March, then got the best of Fiorot, a fellow title contender, at Noche UFC to put herself in position for another title shot.

7. Tatiana Suarez

UFC strawweight

Record: 13-1

Last: W (UD) vs. Virna Jandiroba, Nov. 7

Next: TBA

If Suarez was still feeling the effects of last year's humbling defeat to Zhang Weili in a title challenge, she certainly didn't show it at UFC 327, overcoming early adversity to thrash Loopy Godínez. Then she went on to beat another fellow top-10 strawweight, Jandiroba, sending a message to the division that Suarez is going to be a tough out for anyone at 115 pounds.

8. Dakota Ditcheva

PFL flyweight

Record: 16-0

Last: W (UD) vs. Denise Kielholtz, July 31

Next: TBA

Not only did Ditcheva win the PFL's flyweight season in 2024, but she did so in spectacular fashion -- a TKO finish over Taila Santos, who once challenged for a UFC title. Ditcheva fought only once in 2025, dominating Sumiko Inaba in the co-main event of the first PFL Champions Series card in Cape Town, South Africa. She then spent over a year on the sideline, healing injuries to both hands, before returning at PFL New York with a dominant win over Kielholtz.

9. Manon Fiorot

UFC flyweight

Record: 13-3

Last: L (UD) vs. Alexa Grasso, Sept. 12

Next: TBA

Fiorot had handled everyone the UFC put in front of her -- except the champion, Valentina Shevchenko, who defeated the Frenchwoman at UFC 315 in May 2025. But then, with another title shot within her grasp, Fiorot ran into Grasso, a former champion, at Noche UFC and lost a competitive fight.

10. Jasmine Jasudavicius

UFC flyweight

Record: 16-4

Last: W (UD) vs. Erin Blanchfield, Oct. 17

Next: TBA

Jasudavicius was rising in the 125-pound division until being knocked out by Manon Fiorot last year, halting a five-fight winning streak. But she got back up and won two in a row, most recently an impressive grappling performance against Blanchfield, to reassert herself as a contender.

Other fighter receiving votes: Joselyne Edwards and Virna Jandiroba.

How our panel voted

UFC welterweight champion

Makhachev vacated the UFC lightweight championship to go for a second title at welterweight. By winning that belt last November with a thrashing of Jack Della Maddalena, Makhachev staked his place among MMA's greatest -- not just in today's sport but of all time. UFC featherweight champion

Record: 29-4

It felt as if the sport had started to write Volkanovski's eulogy following his knockout loss to Ilia Topuria in February 2024. Volkanovski noticed and made a point of proving to everyone he still has plenty left by recapturing the featherweight belt at UFC 314, the first of two consecutive wins over Lopes. His age (38) will likely continue to be a prefight topic, which is fine because Volkanovski enjoys proving people wrong. He did just that by handing Evloev his first loss at UFC 333.

What a return to the top it's been for Yan. He began his career with 15 consecutive wins before going on a 1-4 run from 2021 to 2023. That almost doesn't feel real now, after watching him reclaim his throne against Dvalishvili, who once handed him the worst loss of his career, then completing his trilogy with Dvalishvili with a successful title defense. Yan took a major detour, but this was the destination we felt he was capable of before the skid. He once again looks like one of the best fighters on the planet.

4. Ilia Topuria

UFC lightweight

Record: 17-1

Last: L (TKO4) vs. Justin Gaethje, June 14

Next: TBA

Topuria was an undefeated two-division champion when he ran into Gaethje at UFC Freedom 250 and was brutalized in a stoppage loss. How will that affect the immediate future of Topuria? His knockout wins over two of the greatest featherweights, Alexander Volkanovski and Max Holloway, gave him an intimidating aura. Can the former champion get that back?

5. Justin Gaethje

UFC lightweight champion

Record: 28-5

Last: W (TKO4) vs. Ilia Topuria, June 14

Next: TBA

Gaethje has spent his 15-year career thrilling MMA fans, but before the title bout on the White House lawn, all he had to show for it -- aside from 15 bonus checks in 15 UFC appearances -- were two missed opportunities to be an undisputed champion. His fourth-round TKO of Topuria got Gaethje over the hump. It was a resilient performance in a back-and-forth battle that is a prime candidate for fight of the year. More important for Gaethje: At age 37, he is finally sitting at the top of the mountain.

UFC flyweight champion

Record: 18-2

Van has been champion since December, but until UFC 331, there were doubters. Van had been handed the belt by default, when his challenge for the title was waved off after 26 seconds because Pantoja dislocated his left elbow. Van went on to defend the title against Tatsuro Taira in May, then faced Pantoja in a rematch at UFC 331. Van produced a clear victory -- his eighth win in a row -- to leave no doubt who rules at 125 pounds.

7. Ciryl Gane

UFC heavyweight champion

Previous ranking: Tied for 8th

Record: 15-2, 1 NC

Last: W (UD) vs. Josh Hokit, Nov. 14

Next: TBA

Gane is unique in that he is the first -- and could very well go down as the only -- heavyweight to face the division's four biggest names in Francis Ngannou, Jon Jones, Tom Aspinall and Pereira. None of those four have fought each other, yet all four have have fought the Frenchman. Gane was 0-2 with a no-contest against that group before he knocked out Pereira in the second round of their interim title fight on the White House lawn. Gane was elevated to undisputed champ after Aspinall, still injured, vacated his title, and the new champ made his first defense against Hokit at UFC 334, winning a slugfest.

8. Arman Tsarukyan

UFC lightweight

Previous ranking: 7

Record: 24-3

Last: W (KO1) vs. Mauricio Ruffy, Sept. 19

Next: TBA

Tsarukyan is right back in the place he was in January 2025 -- on the cusp of a title fight. He withdrew from a challenge of Islam Makhachev one day before UFC 311 because of a back injury, and later in the year he was passed over twice when the UFC was booking lightweight title bouts. But by knocking out Ruffy with an elbow in the first round at UFC 331, Tsarukyan put himself back at the front of the line.

UFC bantamweight

Record: 21-6

Last: L (UD) vs. Petr Yan, Oct. 24

Next: TBA

Dvalishvili was on one of the most impressive runs through the UFC's bantamweight division ever. Not only did he defeat Sean O'Malley for the second time in nine months at UFC 316, but he showcased a new part of his game, finishing O'Malley with a guillotine. Starting in August 2022, Dvalishvili beat José Aldo, Yan, Henry Cejudo, O'Malley (twice), Umar Nurmagomedov and Cory Sandhagen. But at UFC 323, in an attempt to become the first champion in UFC history to successfully defend a title four times in a calendar year, Dvalishvili lost a rematch with Yan. Their third meeting at UFC 333 was the most competitive in their trilogy, but Dvalishvili fell short again.

Pereira made a big splash in the MMA after a world championship career in kickboxing. He joined the UFC in 2021 and became a middleweight champion the following year, then moved on to be a two-time light heavyweight titlist before making an unprecedented bid for a belt in a third weight class when he fought Game at UFC Freedom 250 for an interim heavyweight title. Pereira got knocked out in that fight, but now he's back on his feet and in position to reclaim his position when he faces a fellow title contender, Pavlovich, at UFC 335.
