stories.headline: As Nike replaces Adidas, is UEFA Champions League star ball on its way out?
stories.summary: Nike will replace Adidas as supplier of UEFA Champions League match balls from next season. Will the famous 'star ball' design soon be no more?
stories.body:
Editor's note: This article was first published on Aug. 26, 2026 and has been updated

The UEFA Champions League and UEFA Women's Champions League match balls will boast a brand new look starting next season after UEFA confirmed on Monday that Nike will be taking over from long-standing provider Adidas as the official supplier for the 2027-28 campaign onwards.

Nike will take the reins for the 2027-28 campaign onward after agreeing a deal to supply the official match balls for all three UEFA club competitions from 2027 to 2031 -- the Champions League, the Europa League and the Conference League. According to The Guardian, that deal is worth around $45 million a year, double the value of the final contract with Adidas.

- Man United, Pochettino's to-do list based on what's gone wrong

- Meet Como's Paz, the heir to Messi's Argentina No. 10 shirt

- Champions League talking points: Are Como the real deal?

With Adidas having supplied the official Champions League match ball since 2001, the "star ball" design has become an emblem of the competition. However, the last we see of the iconic pattern might be in the 2026-27 final.

That's because, as things stand, there are no specific details available as to the designs that Nike has in store. In a statement on Monday, UEFA would only say: "Further details on the match ball designs will be revealed in due course." It is also unclear -- and highly unlikely -- that the American sportswear giant will continue with the star theme popularised by Adidas over the past 25 years, as the German powerhouse reportedly hold the rights to the star ball design.

Nike's designs are therefore likely to be fresh and distinct with the intent of drawing a line under Adidas' tenure as UEFA match ball suppliers while also launching their own, modernised visual identity.

Back in August, Adidas unveiled what will be their final iteration of the "star ball," the preliminary eye-catching colourway of which is currently being used throughout the group phase of the 2026-27 Champions League.

The men's version of the 2026-27 Champions League ball is plastered in a neon-spattered livery that, according to Adidas, has been inspired by players creating colourful moments of magic and personal expression while plugging away at training on cold, foggy training pitches during their quest to attain Champions League greatness.

The design for the women's match ball is a little less abstract. The golden-orange pattern takes its inspiration from the aura of the ring of 11 stars that make up the UWCL emblem, with flashes of metallic purple and silver then adding a dash of visual contrast to the mix.

Both balls are based on the template that Adidas have used for their Champions League match balls since the introduction of the "Finale 1" ball for the 2001-02 season. Since then, over 50 iterations of the UCL star ball have been deployed in the competition -- and that's not including the various hi-vis yellow variants that have been used in winter months over the years.

stories.headline: Sources: MLS side FC Cincy nearing deal to acquire NWSL's Racing
stories.summary: The ownership groups of MLS side FC Cincinnati and the NWSL's Racing Louisville FC are nearing an agreement that would relocate the NWSL team to Cincinnati in 2028, multiple sources told ESPN.
stories.body:
The ownership groups of MLS side FC Cincinnati and the NWSL's Racing Louisville FC are nearing an agreement that would relocate the NWSL team to Cincinnati in 2028, multiple sources told ESPN.

Racing Louisville said in a statement on Tuesday that the team is "actively working through a process to sell" the team, although it did not name a prospective buyer. No agreement has been finalized yet, sources said, and it is not immediately clear what a final sale price could be for the NWSL team.

If a deal is reached, Racing Louisville would play the 2027 NWSL season at Lynn Family Stadium in Louisville, Kentucky, before operations moved 100 miles northeast to Cincinnati in 2028. Once there, Racing would play at TQL Stadium, the 26,000-seat downtown home of the MLS side.

ESPN first reported in September that the two sides were engaged in negotiations.

Soccer Holdings and chairman John Neace own Racing Louisville and began seeking investment earlier this year, as ESPN reported in May.

"As the NWSL has grown, so have the financial demands of competing in the league. Additional investment is needed to support the club's long-term future, and we are actively working through a process to sell Racing to a new ownership group," the Louisville-based club said in a statement Tuesday. "Racing was established to bring top-tier women's professional sports to Louisville -- something meaningful our community could rally around. That vision became reality because of the fans, partners and community members who believed in it and continue to support the club. We are deeply grateful for their roles in making Racing what it is today.

"Further updates will be shared as appropriate. In the meantime, our focus is on supporting our players and staff ahead of the 2027 season."

FC Cincinnati also inquired about purchasing Racing Louisville in recent years, ESPN previously reported. On each previous occasion, however, sources cited personal relationships between ownership groups as an obstacle to a potential sale.

An FC Cincinnati spokesperson provided the following statement to ESPN on Tuesday: "We understand and appreciate the excitement and interest around the possibility of bringing an NWSL team to Cincinnati. The passion for soccer in this community is undeniable, and FC Cincinnati remains deeply committed to supporting the continued growth of the women's game. We are hard at work exploring opportunities to expand our involvement in women's soccer, and we are hopeful to have an update in the near future."

Recently, the situation in Louisville has become more urgent. Racing joined the NWSL ahead of the 2021 NWSL season for an expansion fee of around $2 million. Investment in the league by new owners of other clubs has increased exponentially since then. Expansion teams in Atlanta and Columbus will begin playing in the NWSL in 2028 after paying $165 million and $205 million fees, respectively.

Sources told ESPN that throughout the year NWSL commissioner Jessica Berman has been heavily involved in the process of finding a solution in Louisville.

"Their ownership group has made clear that they are prepared to sell," NWSL commissioner Jessica Berman told ESPN in August. "The trajectory of this league has an investment thesis. Our owners, and the future of the league, need to be aligned in that investment thesis.

"They [Louisville] have made clear that they're not prepared to sign up for that. And so, they're raising capital because they want more financial support to be able to invest in the team, which is an indication of their understanding of what's required."

Racing Louisville averaged just under 5,500 fans per game this year, down slightly from 2025. Only the Chicago Stars averaged fewer fans per game.

Sources across the league said to ESPN that Columbus' $205 million price tag paid earlier this year ostensibly sets a floor for any future team, while adding that the NWSL is exercising caution about any potential sale price for a relocation of Racing Louisville to Cincinnati since those cities are only about 100 miles apart.

FC Cincinnati unsuccessfully bid for a 2026 NWSL expansion team with a group that, at the time, included WNBA star Caitlin Clark. Denver was ultimately awarded that team, the NWSL's 14th, for $110 million.

Racing Louisville was recently valued at $127 million and $140 million by Sportico and Forbes, respectively, ranking it as one of the least valuable franchises in the NWSL.

"Relocation should be a last resort," Berman said in March about her philosophy at large. "We view, in our philosophy of what our teams are, is driven by the idea that these are community assets. And what that means is that the community has to believe and it has to be demonstrated over time, that owners and the league will keep these teams in markets even through periods of transition, team sales, or other ups and downs that might be happening with the club, with their on-field performance.

"That does not mean that it's a red line. It means that we will only consider that under appropriate circumstances, and we will be very judicious and exercise high discretion in those circumstances where we feel that it's appropriate."

Versions of relocation have happened in the past in the NWSL. The North Carolina Courage were previously the Western New York Flash until moving in January of 2017. The NWSL also had a franchise leave Kansas City for Salt Lake City, Utah, then return to Kansas City. Both markets now have teams after the Utah Royals were revived in 2024.

stories.headline: Toronto Tempo win 2027 WNBA draft lottery, land No. 1 pick
stories.summary: The Tempo won the WNBA draft lottery Sunday night, earning the No. 1 pick and potentially the chance to draft USC star JuJu Watkins. The Comets will choose second, followed by the Mystics.
stories.body:
The Toronto Tempo will have the No. 1 pick in the 2027 WNBA draft after winning the draft lottery Sunday night.

After completing its inaugural season in 2026, Toronto becomes the first franchise to have the top pick heading into its second season since the Dream in 2009, when Atlanta selected Angel McCoughtry. The Tempo will make their selection April 12.

Lottery odds are based on teams' two-year cumulative records, except for Portland and Toronto, which were expansion teams in 2026. Their odds were solely based on their records from this past season.

The Houston Comets, formerly the Connecticut Sun (22-66), and Toronto (11-33) had the best odds to land the No. 1 pick, each with 329 chances out of 1,000. This marked the first time since 2015 that two teams had the same odds for the first selection.

The Sun, relocating to Texas from Connecticut this offseason, went 1-2 against Toronto in 2026 -- which is the first tiebreaker -- so the franchise couldn't fall past the third pick. Toronto was guaranteed at least the fourth selection.

"I [felt] like something amazing was going to happen," said Tempo forward Aneesah Morrow, the team's lottery representative. "We're here now ... The future is bright. We have great and amazing players, and we have a country on our back. It feels different when you play like that."

Houston will select second in the draft. All of the other selections are in line with what the odds projected heading into Sunday. Washington, which had the next-best odds after acquiring Chicago's first-round pick in the trade that sent Ariel Atkins to the Sky, will pick third.

Seattle will select at No. 4, followed by Portland at No. 5. The Los Angeles Sparks have the sixth and seventh picks -- one that is their own and the other acquired from Phoenix in the Kelsey Plum trade in August.

USC's JuJu Watkins is projected to go No. 1 in ESPN's latest mock draft released Thursday, with Texas' Madison Booker slotted at No. 2.

Notre Dame's Hannah Hidalgo, Virginia's Kymora Johnson, LSU's Mikaylah Williams, Kansas' S'Mya Nichols and Sarah Cisse of France are projected to round out the lottery picks.

The Tempo had a strong start to their season before veteran Brittney Sykes was sidelined indefinitely because of a plantar fascia injury. After she went down, Toronto went 4-21, including a 12-game losing streak. But Sykes and Marina Mabrey combined to form one of the highest-scoring backcourts in the league.

Toronto has some young talent in Morrow, whom the team acquired in a midseason trade, and last year's No. 6 pick Kiki Rice, who was the team's third-leading scorer but missed nearly two months because of a Grade 2 left ankle sprain. The combination of Mabrey, Sykes and Rice gives the Tempo perimeter depth. However, they are somewhat thin in the front court.

"[Toronto] is amazing," Morrow said. "Ever since I walked in the locker room, from the beginning, I was able to see the chemistry ... it's all about building the future of the Toronto franchise."

The WNBA schedule will increase from 44 to 50 games in the 2027 season, making it the longest in league history. The added games were part of the new collective bargaining agreement, which also vastly increased pay, secured a $2.2 billion media deal and slated six expansion teams to join the league between 2024 and 2030.

The 2027 WNBA season is expected to start May 7 and has a latest possible end date of Oct. 24, sources told ESPN's Alexa Philippou last week.

"We're excited about the momentum; it's never been stronger," said Bethany Donaphin, senior vice president and head of WNBA league operations. "We think there's a demand, and we're excited to expand to 50 games."

The rest of the first-round draft order is: No. 8 New York, No. 9 Dallas, No. 10 Indiana, No. 11 Chicago, No. 12 Chicago, No. 13 Dallas, No. 14 Golden State and No. 15 Minnesota.

stories.headline: Kangaroos bounce Kiwis for fourth-straight Rugby League World Cup title
stories.summary: The Kangaroos have won a fourth-straight Rugby League World Cup, toppling New Zealand 32-12 in Brisbane.
stories.body:
The Kangaroos have punished a disappointing New Zealand, with Reece Walsh running riot in a 32-12 World Cup final waltz.

There was an expectation the Kiwis, searching for their second Cup title and first since 2008, would push Australia all the way after a two-point loss in a pulsating tournament opener.

But the visitors struggled from the outset in Brisbane on Sunday night, Jamayne Isaako's kick-off floating long in a sign of things to come.

Walsh dazzled at fullback for the Kangaroos, his pace, vision and wicked footwork too much as he helped lay on two tries and generally wreak havoc around the ruck and close to the line.

Conversely, Walsh's New Zealand opposite Kalyn Ponga -- International Rugby League's Golden Boot winner on Thursday night -- was unable to get into game.

Australian hooker Harry Grant and halves Tom Dearden and Cam Munster completely outplayed their error-riddled opposites, while the Kangaroos' pack muscled up.

Dearden laid on two first-half tries for Liam Martin with well-timed short balls, while Bradman Best was rewarded for an inspired chase-down tackle of Jahrome Hughes with a try soon after.

When Tom Trbojevic scored to begin the second half it was 28-6 and effectively game over.

Jack Bostock completed his breakout season with a try in each half for Australia.

It was the Kangaroos' fourth consecutive title and 10th in the last 11 tournaments, dating back to 1975.

stories.headline: Mauricio Pochettino: Man United players must relearn 'about being winners'
stories.summary: Mauricio Pochettino has said his first job as Manchester United's new head coach is to remind the players how to win after a miserable start to the season.
stories.body:
Mauricio Pochettino has said his first job as Manchester United's new head coach is to remind the players how to win after a miserable start to the season.

Pochettino began work at Carrington on Wednesday after taking over from Michael Carrick. He's inherited a team 18th in the table with just one Premier League win all season.

The 54-year-old will take charge for the first time against Liverpool at Anfield on Sunday and ahead of the game, he said his players must quickly rediscover the feeling of winning matches.

"The most important thing is for us to start to work hard to recover those feelings about being winners, to win games, to perform," Pochettino said in his first full interview since his appointment.

"But that is not only to talk about winning, it is about starting to act and to change things and to try to affect in a good way all the areas to try to really believe that we can recover that feeling to win."

A run of eight league games without a win has seen United slip into the Premier League's bottom three. Their worst start to a season for 40 years has raised the possibility of relegation to the second tier.

But Pochettino insists he doesn't want his squad playing with that pressure on their shoulders and instead told the players to "express their talent."

"I think it is a mistake to see the situation," he said.

"We need to see the potential of this club. Of course, circumstances are circumstances and we need to be responsible of the circumstances.

- Manchester United finally get Mauricio Pochettino after a decade of near misses

- Predicting how all 20 Premier League teams will finish the season

- Mauricio Pochettino arrives at Man United: 'You will see, give me time'

"The players need to express their talent. We need to create the environment and the platform for the players to perform. That is the most important thing and that is our priority now, is to work with them and try to take the pressure.

"Pressure needs to bring energy. Responsibility needs to bring energy because if not, it is too heavy to put all that pressure and responsibility on your back."

Pochettino: Sir Alex Ferguson 'the best' in history

Pochettino has been close to joining United in the past and was interviewed for the job in 2024 shortly after leaving Chelsea.

Finally in the hot seat after signing a contract until 2029, he revealed his affinity for the club began more than 25 years ago when he attended the 1999 Champions League final victory over Bayern Munich in Barcelona, while he was a player for Espanyol.

"That was an iconic final," he said.

"From there I was so excited to see Manchester United and more with the admiration for Sir Alex Ferguson. For me, the best coach in the history of the sport. Now being the head coach is an honour and a privilege. The excitement to be here is massive."

Man United can escape relegation zone under Pochettino

Pochettino arrives at United to find them in the Premier League relegation zone. One point behind 17th-placed Coventry City, a victory in Pochettino's first match against Liverpool this weekend could be enough to take United clear of the drop-zone.

stories.headline: Are there actually 32 true starting quarterbacks in the NFL at any given time?
stories.summary: Finding legit quarterbacks can be tough, and many people think there aren't even enough true QB1s to fill the league's 32 QB1 spots. Is there any validity to that?
stories.body:
It has been an absolutely brutal year for quarterback injuries in the NFL. When I wrote about this in September, the 2026 season was already looking as if it could be on the high end for missing signal-callers. And as we hit Week 11, it's almost more difficult to find teams that haven't had to go to their backups than ones who have been able to stick with their starter all season.

Fourteen teams have been unable to play their primary quarterback for more than a quarter of work because of an injury this season. The Bears, Cardinals and Ravens have been forced to turn to their third-string option. As many as seven of the 10 afternoon games Sunday will feature at least one backup quarterback.

Though both the league and its teams are desperate to keep the best quarterbacks healthy, injuries are going to happen. And in just about every case, going from a starter to a backup is going to create problems. Over the past decade -- without factoring in any other information -- teams that got a full game from their starting quarterback and went up against opposition that didn't get a single snap from their preferred starter won nearly 66% of the time.

Subscribe: 'The Bill Barnwell Show'

It would be great if teams could turn to a deep pool of backups, but that just isn't the case at quarterback. And there's a phrase that comes up all the time: "There aren't 32 starting-caliber quarterbacks to go around in the NFL." And yes, the reality is that the league rarely, if ever, has 32 quality starters featuring at the same time.

But does that mean that there couldn't be 32 quality starters if they were dispersed around the league's 32 teams? I'm not so sure. There are some gaps in that logic, and it's a topic I've always wanted to explore. The middle of an injury-riddled 2026 season feels like the right time to get there. How many viable starting QBs are typically on NFL rosters at any one time? Is it 20? 30? 40?

I wasn't sure of the answer, but I'm sure we're not considering the question correctly. I'm going to show why that's the case and give my best estimate for how many viable quarterbacks have typically been present on NFL rosters at any one time over the past few decades.

Jump to:

Why the argument is flawed

True QB1s in a typical season

What it means for 2026

Why the argument is flawed
The fundamental flaw in the "There aren't 32 starting-caliber quarterbacks" argument is that it evaluates only the 32 quarterbacks who are currently playing in NFL lineups. Even if we ignore injuries and just consider each team's ideal and preferred option heading into 2026, that's still going to leave us with a handful of teams that don't have a quarterback who projects to be even a viable starter, let alone a solid one. At any one time, there are typically going to be at least a couple of replacement-level starters in a starting lineup. By midseason, when injuries have usually hit the league, those concerns feel even more acute.

On the other hand, there are a lot of reasons why the 32 starting quarterbacks in the league at any given time aren't the 32 best options to fill those roles.

Teams aren't as good at identifying the right starting QBs as we'd like to believe. When it comes its quarterbacks, NFL teams are generally meritocratic and able to identify who they should be starting by the end of training camp. But not always.

Some teams are locked into long-term contracts for players and want to give that passer every chance to prove that he's worth his deal. The Browns started Deshaun Watson to open the 2024 season and got historically bad play for seven games before the highly paid veteran tore his Achilles. Jameis Winston isn't a superstar, but the Browns were a much better offense the moment he entered the lineup.

Other teams are operating in the opposite boat and have a young, highly drafted quarterback who isn't very good yet playing ahead of a veteran backup who would be more effective if given the full-time starting role. Also in 2024, the Colts were starting Anthony Richardson Sr. ahead of Joe Flacco for most of the season despite the fact that Flacco had helped lead the Browns to the postseason the previous season. Richardson plays a very different style, but if the goal was just to field the best possible quarterback, Flacco probably should have been the choice.

Teams also just flat-out make evaluation mistakes, even with players they've already seen in their offense. The Vikings chose Kyler Murray, Carson Wentz and Max Brosmer ahead of J.J. McCarthy and then traded their 2024 first-round pick to the Giants, where he has been a much more productive player than any of the signal-callers he had been competing with in camp. I'm sure some of that was a product of not wanting to deal with McCarthy as a third or fourth quarterback, but strictly in terms of on-field performance, the Vikings appear to have chosen the wrong guys.

In the big picture, teams find it even more difficult to identify which quarterback prospects will succeed as they enter the NFL, even when those guys are roughly entering the league within the same tier. In 2018, five QBs came off the board in Round 1. Baker Mayfield, who has been somewhere between a solid starter and a replacement-level passer in his various stops around the league, was the first pick. Sam Darnold, who fits the same mold, was next. Josh Allen, a future Hall of Famer, followed. The Cardinals then chose Josh Rosen, who was out of football after 16 starts, before the Ravens took Lamar Jackson, who will join Allen in Canton one day.

I'll get to later-round picks in a moment, but the idea that the 32 quarterbacks starting around the league at any given time are actually the 32 best quarterbacks in football simply isn't true. And it takes a few seconds to quickly look around the league to see that.

Some teams have no viable quarterback, but others have more than one. There are going to be some QB1s this weekend who either haven't proved themselves to be NFL starters or previously weren't able to perform like one. Players like Tommy DeVito and Joe Milton probably don't qualify as viable starting quarterbacks for the purposes of the statement we're evaluating, even if they're going to be on the field Sunday. Of course, they're replacing quarterbacks who are hurt in Drake Maye and Jalen Hurts, respectively, who would comfortably fit any definition of a quality starter.

Elsewhere, there are teams that haven't needed to turn to a backup but might have two viable starters. The Bengals have Flacco backing up Joe Burrow. Marcus Mariota has been solid behind Jayden Daniels as an injury replacement in Washington. Joshua Dobbs put together an impressive run with the Vikings in 2023 and hasn't been needed behind Jared Goff in Detroit. Murray has been disappointing in Minnesota, but he was a solid starter for the Cardinals over the past half-decade. Drew Lock has been effective filling in for Darnold in Seattle. And Mac Jones was able to sustain the offense for the 49ers when Brock Purdy was injured last season.

Are all of those guys stars? No. But if the goal was to pick the 32 best quarterbacks in football in 2026, backups like Flacco, Jones and Mariota would probably be in that conversation ahead of some starters around the NFL, even though they're backing up other high-profile quarterbacks and aren't currently in starting roles. And we've seen each of those backups push teams to the postseason as starters in the past, which would seem to suggest that they would be viable starters again in the right situation.

Some players would be starter-worthy in certain schemes and ineffective in others.

If we were looking for quarterbacks who would excel in every single scheme and situation, regardless of their individual skill set, that number will be very low. That's also true for many other positions, too, though, and we don't talk about scarcity in those spots in the same way. Guard Kevin Dotson was struggling in a Steelers scheme that asked him to move laterally in a zone-heavy run game. After being traded to the Rams and put in a gap-heavy run game, where he is moving vertically and overpowering linemen at 6-foot-4 and 328 pounds, Dotson has been a Pro Bowl-caliber interior lineman.

In years past, identifying quarterbacks who were useful in one scheme or situation and seemingly useless in another would have been an abstract argument. In 2026, it's obvious. If you were evaluating the league's passers while Darnold was stuck playing for the Jets or Panthers, the idea that he could be an above-average starter would have been comical. On the Vikings and Seahawks, with the right playmaker(s) and in play-action heavy offenses? Darnold has been a changed man, presiding over a 13-win Vikings team before going to the Seahawks and winning a Super Bowl.

Others have looked hopeless in one offense and helpful in another over a 12-month span. McCarthy going from the Vikings to the Giants. Mayfield going from the Panthers to the Rams and then the Buccaneers. Mac Jones going from the Jaguars to the 49ers. Kirk Cousins going from the Falcons to the Raiders. Daniel Jones going from the Giants in 2024 to the Colts in 2025. Context and situation matter, and there are a lot more players who are going to look functional with solid playmakers, line play and good coaching around them.

This also extends over the course of a player's career. Geno Smith looked overwhelmed early in his career with the Jets, then spent the next seven years marked as a backup incapable of doing a solid job as a starter. It took Russell Wilson getting injured and traded and the Seahawks giving Smith a real shot at a starting job in a competition with Lock in 2022 to prove that he was a useful QB1. And Smith then went through this same cycle over the past 12 months, struggling badly on a Raiders team that had little infrastructure before playing much better so far this season with the Jets.

So ... does that mean that there aren't 32 viable quarterbacks? Or just that there aren't 32 viable places for a quarterback to succeed? Stick Josh Allen on the Dolphins or Titans, and he's going to elevate the offense on what they have now -- but he's not going to singlehandedly turn them into what the Bills are capable of doing on a weekly basis. Is Mac Jones a realistic starting quarterback because he has looked good on the 49ers and in his first year with the Patriots, or is he something less because of the time when he struggled in New England and Jacksonville?

Some players haven't had the chance to prove themselves ... and others never do.

This is the one that's impossible to prove. In a perfect world, every quarterback would get a chance to prove himself at the highest level with real reps against legitimate defenses to show whether they can succeed. In the 1980s and 1990s, quarterbacks were able to get NFL opportunities by thriving in other professional leagues. Even leaving aside Jim Kelly and Steve Young, who were already highly touted prospects and first-round picks before detouring to the USFL on their way to Hall of Fame careers, others went on more circuitous paths. Warren Moon, Doug Flutie and others parlayed success in the CFL into the NFL. And the likes of Jake Delhomme, Brad Johnson and Jon Kitna got meaningful reps in NFL Europe in the mid-1990s before emerging as useful starters stateside.

In the modern version of the league? First-round picks get an extended chance, while second- and third-rounders usually get at least a couple of starts (sometimes more) by the end of their rookie deal. Day 3 selections and undrafted free agents? Good luck. It's entirely possible that they might enter and exit the NFL without ever getting more than a stray snap or two in garbage time.

Is it because those guys aren't NFL-caliber starters? In many cases, I'm sure that's true. When you think about the late-round picks who have built significant careers as pro quarterbacks, though, it's usually because they were forced into the lineup by injuries and got an extended chance to prove themselves. Let's consider how some of the most notable Day 3 picks and undrafted free agents got into the starting lineup:

Kurt Warner toiled in Arena Football and in NFL Europe in the mid-90s before catching on as a third-stringer with the Rams. After a handful of snaps in 1998, the Rams left Warner unprotected in the expansion draft, signed Trent Green to be their starter and used a fourth-round pick on Joe Germaine, suggesting that they didn't see Warner as a long-term solution or even a significant backup. Green tore his ACL just before the start of the 1999 season, forcing Warner into the lineup. He threw for 4,353 yards and 41 touchdowns, won league MVP and led the Rams to a Super Bowl victory. He won another MVP award two years later, made two more trips to the Super Bowl and landed in the Hall of Fame.
Tom Brady threw three passes as a rookie sixth-round pick in 2000 with the Patriots, with Bill Belichick acknowledging that the Patriots were deciding between Brady and Tim Rattay on Day 3 of that year's draft. There's a cottage industry around people who insist they knew Brady was going to be a superstar, but in March 2001, the Patriots signed Drew Bledsoe to a 10-year, $103 million contract, with Robert Kraft saying that it was an opportunity to sign "... one of the great Patriots for the rest of his career." Well, you know what happened. Bledsoe suffered a serious chest injury on a hit by Mo Lewis in Week 2. Brady took over and stunningly led the Patriots to a Super Bowl. The Pats traded Bledsoe to the Bills, and Brady became the greatest player in league history.

Dak Prescott wasn't the first choice for the Cowboys in the 2016 draft, as Jerry Jones wanted to draft Paxton Lynch and Connor Cook, only to be beaten to the punch by the Broncos and Raiders, respectively. The Cowboys settled for Prescott in the fourth round. He played well in the preseason, but he wasn't going to push Tony Romo (who was on a massive contract) out of the lineup. When Romo injured his back during a preseason game, it opened the door for Prescott. He posted a 104.9 passer rating as a rookie and beat out backfield mate Ezekiel Elliott to win Offensive Rookie of the Year. Romo threw four passes late in the season and never played again.
Brock Purdy was the last pick of the 2022 draft. The 49ers were impressed by what they saw in training camp, but they had already committed to Trey Lance, their 2021 first-round pick, as their quarterback of the future. When Lance went down because of a fractured ankle early in the 2022 season, the 49ers turned to former starter Jimmy Garoppolo -- not Purdy -- suggesting that they didn't really believe Purdy was the best quarterback on the roster. Purdy eventually took over for an injured Garoppolo and was a revelation down the stretch before injuring his elbow in the NFC title game. Installed as the starter in 2023, Purdy was an MVP contender and took the 49ers to the Super Bowl. He's playing at that level again in 2026.

This isn't always the case. Romo impressed Bill Parcells and Sean Payton as an undrafted free agent and took over for Bledsoe. Matt Hasselbeck came out of a quarterback factory in Green Bay and got an extended chance in Seattle. But typically, in the post-NFL Europe era, late-round picks and undrafted guys rack up starts only by getting an opportunity via a long-term injury to the starter or by moving around the league as a journeyman, like Ryan Fitzpatrick and Brian Hoyer.

It seems incredibly unlikely that the only four late-round picks and undrafted free agents capable of producing elite-caliber play over the past 30 years were all fortunate enough to have the starter ahead of them suffer a significant injury.

But what if those stars hadn't gotten those opportunities? Brady's first start was a victory, but he threw for 168 yards before going 12-of-24 for 86 yards in a loss to the Dolphins the following week. What if Bledsoe had simply pulled a hamstring and was ready to come back after two weeks? Would Brady have gotten another significant opportunity? Does he end up getting three or four starts down the line for a bad team as he toils as a backup? What if the Cowboys had drafted Lynch, and Prescott ended up going to the Bills, who were the next team to take a quarterback in 2016? What if Green had stayed healthy and Warner spent another year as a backup before deciding he was sick of the grind and retiring?

And just as importantly, how many great quarterbacks are out there who never got an opportunity? I can't sit here and tell you that Garrett Nussmeier, Haynes King and Kurtis Rourke are future stars, because we haven't seen them play at the pro level for any extended period of time. Chances are most Day 3 picks and undrafted free agents aren't high-level quarterbacks. But it would be naive to believe that there aren't at least one or two who would be able to thrive if given the chance.

Some options aren't in the NFL.

There are usually at least one or two starting-caliber quarterbacks who aren't actually playing in the NFL. Some are retired but still capable of playing at a reasonable level. I'm not sure there are any current retired quarterbacks who would qualify, but if Matthew Stafford retired after the 2026 season, I still think it would be fair to consider him a solid QB1 for the 2027 campaign for the purposes of counting our 32.

And then, on the flip side, there might be the occasional quarterback at the college level who would theoretically be capable of stepping in and holding his own as a pro. We've seen a number of rookies immediately step in as top-10 quarterbacks as pros in recent years, including Andrew Luck, Jayden Daniels and C.J. Stroud. Could those guys instead have been viable starters in the NFL during their final year in school? Could someone like Trevor Lawrence, who won a national title as a freshman at Clemson, have been a pro passer in 2019 or 2020 before entering the league in 2021?

So, how many viable quarterbacks are there in a typical season?
Having laid out why I think we're underestimating the number of true starting quarterbacks, I attempted to calculate how many have been on rosters in a typical season in the 32-team era, which started in 2002.

To qualify as a viable quarterback, I picked signal-callers who had posted an adjusted net yards per attempt index (ANY/A+) of 100 or better over a 200-attempt season within three years of the season in question. Adjusted net yards per attempt index is a Pro Football Reference metric. Adjusted net yards per attempt improves on passer rating by weighting passing yardage, touchdowns and interceptions more accurately while also including sacks and sack yardage. The index element scales performance to the rest of the league each year, so an average performance is always 100.

In other words, we're looking for quarterbacks who have produced about a half-season of league-average play as evidence that they would be viable options. Since not every quarterback gets a chance to play each year, and quarterbacks can be influenced by situation, we're also looking back three years to see if there's a solid performance in that QB's past. For instance, Mac Jones hasn't played this season, but his effectiveness on 289 pass attempts for the 49ers a year ago is enough for me to believe that he could be a legit option if given an opportunity now. Likewise, a healthy Lamar Jackson would obviously still be a very good starter, even if he doesn't qualify because he hasn't been able to get on the field and throw very often this season.

And since quarterbacks can be useful before they ever get a chance to contribute or get in the right place to play well, I'm also willing to consider passers who post a solid half-season up to three years in the future as reasonable options. If we were evaluating signal-callers in 2022, we wouldn't have known much about Jordan Love's pro viability, given that he had thrown 87 pro passes by the end of his second season. Given that Love quickly proved himself to be a useful starter after taking over in 2023, though, it seems realistic to consider him as an effective option in 2022.

There are limitations here. I'm not including seasons for quarterbacks who weren't in the NFL or those who had retired, so Jayden Daniels' excellent 2024 campaign doesn't mean I'm automatically counting him as a viable starter in 2021, 2022 or 2023. And likewise, while Russell Wilson was an adequate low-end starter for the Steelers in 2024, I'm not counting him as a realistic option in 2026 given his retirement.

There will be quarterbacks who either make a major leap early in their career or fall off a cliff at the end, and it's possible that they might not be as viable as this method suggests. Simultaneously, I'm not including those quarterbacks who were outside of the league, even if they might realistically be able to play at a starter level. I'm also not including players who haven't yet proved themselves or never got a chance to show what they could do, even though I strongly suspect there are more functional starters in that group than you might think.

The answer is 39. I'd estimate that there are about 39 viable quarterbacks who could handle a starting role in the NFL at any given time over the past 25 years. That number has been in a relatively consistent band, dropping as low as 36 (which is where it was in 2025) and as high as 44 (in 2006). That's down from an average of 44 in the 1990s, which I would chalk up to teams being more aggressive benching their starters and more opportunities to evaluate potential backups in NFL Europe and other secondary leagues.

What does that look like in practice? Is it too simplistic? Let's take a look at 2022, when there were 37 qualified quarterbacks by this method. How did they prove they were able to go?

Useful in 2022 (19): Josh Allen, Tom Brady, Jacoby Brissett, Joe Burrow, Derek Carr, Kirk Cousins, Andy Dalton, Jimmy Garoppolo, Jared Goff, Taylor Heinicke, Justin Herbert, Jalen Hurts, Lamar Jackson, Trevor Lawrence, Patrick Mahomes, Dak Prescott, Geno Smith, Tua Tagovailoa and Ryan Tannehill

Each of those guys posted a ANY/A+ of 100 or better on a 200-plus pass sample in 2022. Most of them don't require much explanation. Dalton was solid across 14 starts for the Saints, completing two-thirds of his passes and averaging 7.6 yards per attempt. Heinicke was just over the threshold, and I'm not sure he would be on my list, but the journeyman did go 5-3-1 with reasonable numbers as he rotated in with Carson Wentz for the Commanders.

Useful both before and after 2022 (8): Joe Flacco, Mac Jones, Marcus Mariota, Baker Mayfield, Kyler Murray, Aaron Rodgers, Matthew Stafford, Russell Wilson

These eight quarterbacks provided meaningful production as starters both before and after 2022 but weren't able to put together that sort of campaign in 2022. Rodgers took a major step backward after winning back-to-back MVP awards in 2020 and 2021 before producing a season just above league average with the Steelers in 2025. Wilson was enduring a frustrating first year with the Broncos, but he had been productive with the Seahawks in 2021. Stafford sat out half the season because of injuries after winning the Super Bowl the previous season and had an MVP campaign in his future. Murray followed back-to-back Pro Bowl seasons by struggling and then tearing his ACL. In the right situations and with their health, these quarterbacks probably would have been fine or better as starters.

Useful before 2022 (5): Teddy Bridgewater, Gardner Minshew II, Matt Ryan, Deshaun Watson, Carson Wentz

Would all of these guys have been viable options in the right spot in 2022? Bridgewater had been fantastic filling in for Drew Brees in 2019 before producing league-average lines with the Panthers in 2020 and Broncos in 2021. Minshew was producing above-average play with the Eagles, but it was in a backup role. Ryan was on his way out of the league with a dismal Colts team, where he had taken over for Wentz. Were they hopeless? Maybe. But Wentz had thrown 27 touchdowns against seven picks for the Colts in 2020, and Ryan had been right around league average in each of the two previous years for the Falcons. I'm not sure either QB was going to elevate a bad team, but I don't think it's unrealistic to suggest that they could have been passable starters in the right situation.

Watson was suspended for most of the season, but his last full campaign had been in 2020, when he led the league with 4,823 passing yards, leading the Browns to trade multiple first-round picks to acquire him. He has a case for arguing that past performance can still indicate some semblance of future success, even well down the line. Though he sat out significant time because of shoulder and Achilles injuries, he has returned to the Browns' lineup in 2026 and been a slightly below-average starter for the Browns, posting a 96 ANY/A+ six seasons after his last above-average mark in 2020.

Proved to be useful after 2022 (5): Jake Browning, Sam Darnold, Daniel Jones, Jordan Love, Brock Purdy

Browning's the one guy who doesn't pass the smell test for me. Then again, he completed nearly 71% of his passes and averaged 8 yards per attempt filling in for Joe Burrow with the Bengals in 2023. Negative plays were a problem for Browning in 2023 and were an even bigger issue when he got back on the field in 2025, which is why he's on the Chargers practice squad at the moment. I'd argue the positive plays are proof Browning deserves an NFL roster spot, and it's still a pretty small sample, but he's probably not an NFL starter.

The other guys all fit here. Jones was in the middle of a resurgent season with the Giants, where he finished with a 98 ANY/A+; he would get over the 100 mark in his half-season with the Colts in 2025. Love emerged as an above-average starter the following year. Purdy was in the lineup by the end of 2022 but didn't get enough pass attempts to qualify before the end of the regular season. And Darnold had not been able to produce a competent season as a starter to this point as a pro, which would have made the idea that he was a solid starter a bit of a joke at the time. But he proved himself to be a solid option in 2024 with the Vikings. I'm willing to believe that he would have been useful in the right spot in 2022.

That's 37. And while I'd probably exclude Browning and potentially Heinicke from the group, this doesn't include Philip Rivers, who had been productive as a starter with the Colts in 2020 before retiring. Jameis Winston had posted a 114 ANY/A+ in seven starts with the Saints in 2021 before tearing his ACL, coming 39 passes short of qualifying for our list. Mitchell Trubisky had posted a 103 ANY/A+ while going to the playoffs with the Bears in 2018 and came up just short of that mark in 2020 with a 97 ANY/A+. C.J. Stroud, who was immediately a Pro Bowl pick as a rookie in 2023, was throwing for 3,688 yards and 41 touchdowns in his final year at Ohio State in 2022.

And again, this doesn't include any of the unknowns for players who were buried on depth charts and never got a true chance to play. Is the right 2022 number 36? Maybe 38? Perhaps even 40? I feel confident that it's both somewhere in that ballpark and more than 32.

What does that mean for 2026 and beyond?
One conclusion I would generally draw is that despite Tom Moore's famous quote about backup quarterbacks, there are more competent quarterbacks floating around the NFL than it might seem. Not all of those guys are of the same caliber, but the Eagles winning a Super Bowl with Nick Foles under center should put any idea of backups being hopeless to rest. Foles might not have looked great with the Rams after leaving Philadelphia the first time (or the Bears and Jags after leaving the second time), but in the right situation for a limited amount of time, he was fantastic.

One interpretation would be to suggest that teams should be more aggressive trying to take swings on quarterbacks who either haven't played or who aren't perceived as up to starting-standard. That's easy to say from my perspective when I'm not the one who has my job riding on the line, but history is littered with quarterbacks who were perceived to be backups but then thrived in the right role or once given a real opportunity.

It's probably too early to write off someone like Justin Fields or Spencer Rattler. And even someone like Mitchell Trubisky is probably more capable of delivering a solid season in the right role than we might believe. That seems outlandish right now given that Trubisky has generally struggled since leaving the Bears, but it wouldn't be a dramatically different case from Darnold, who was even worse early in his career as a top-three pick before eventually emerging as a Super Bowl-winning starter in Seattle.

More than anything, though, the range of quarterbacks who have thrived in the right situation makes the importance of creating that favorable opportunity so clear. The Vikings have shown over the past year that you can't just plug any quarterback into a situation with good playmakers and a solid offensive line and thrive, but there were several borderline starters who were able to move the ball and revitalize their career in Minnesota. The same thing has happened in San Francisco under Kyle Shanahan.

Though I'm not advocating that a team should blindly dump their starting quarterback for a cheap replacement so they can stock up the rest of the roster with talent, there's something to be said for leaning more toward infrastructure over quarterback when it gets to more marginal cases or paying average-or-worse starters significant money. The difference between, say, Daniel Jones and Marcus Mariota probably isn't the $43 million or so difference in cash that they'll make in 2026. And spending that money on infrastructure around the quarterback makes it more likely that either of those players would succeed in the right role if healthy.

Charlotte Hornets (4-10, 12th in the Eastern Conference) vs. Atlanta Hawks (9-6, fifth in the Eastern Conference)


Atlanta; Friday, 7 p.m. EST


BOTTOM LINE: The Charlotte Hornets travel to play the Charlotte Hornets in an NBA Cup in-season tournament group play matchup.


The Hawks are 4-1 against opponents in the Southeast Division. Atlanta is 2-0 in games decided by less than 4 points.


The Hornets have gone 4-7 against Eastern Conference opponents. Charlotte has a 3-6 record against teams above .500.


The 117.7 points per game the Hawks average are 7.3 more points than the Hornets allow (110.4). The Hawks average 100.1 points per game, 15.7 fewer points than the 115.8 the Hawks give up to opponents.


The teams square off for the second time this season. The Hawks won the last matchup 128-81 on Oct. 23. Jalen Johnson scored 19 points to help lead the Hawks to the victory.


TOP PERFORMERS: Johnson is averaging 19.2 points, 9.3 rebounds and 7.6 assists for the Hawks. Nickeil Alexander-Walker is averaging 3.5 made 3-pointers over the last 10 games.


Naz Reid is averaging 17.6 points and 8.4 rebounds for the Hornets. Brandon Miller is averaging 14.2 points over the past 10 games.


LAST 10 GAMES: Hawks: 7-3, averaging 116.5 points, 47.1 rebounds, 30.3 assists, 10.3 steals and 4.0 blocks per game while shooting 44.1% from the field. Their opponents have averaged 116.1 points per game.


Hornets: 1-9, averaging 98.6 points, 46.4 rebounds, 22.2 assists, 7.2 steals and 4.3 blocks per game while shooting 40.0% from the field. Their opponents have averaged 110.2 points.
